locator.heading: And Thousand-Leal

source_text:
_Descript._] IT hath many long leaves spread upon the ground, finely
cut, and divided into many small parts. Its flowers are white, but not
all of a whiteness and stayed in knots, upon divers green stalks which
rise from among the leaves.

_Place._] It is frequent in all pastures.

_Time._] It flowers late, even in the latter end of August.

_Government and virtues._] It is under the influence of Venus. An
ointment of them cures wounds, and is most fit for such as have
inflammations, it being an herb of Dame Venus; it stops the terms in
women, being boiled in white wine, and the decoction drank; as also the
bloody flux; the ointment of it is not only good for green wounds, but
also for ulcers and fistulas, especially such as abound with moisture.
It stays the shedding of hair, the head being bathed with the decoction
of it; inwardly taken it helps the retentive faculty of the stomach: it
helps the gonorrhea in men, and the whites in women, and helps such as
cannot hold their water; and the leaves chewed in the mouth eases the
tooth-ache, and these virtues being put together, shew the herb to be
drying and binding. Achilles is supposed to be the first that left the
virtues of this herb to posterity, having learned them of this master
Chiron, the Centaur; and certainly a very profitable herb it is in
cramps, and therefore called Militaris.

DIRECTIONS FOR MAKING SYRUPS, CONSERVES,

_&c._ _&c._

HAVING in divers places of this Treatise promised you the way of making
Syrups, Conserves, Oils, Ointments, &c., of herbs, roots, flowers, &c.
whereby you may have them ready for your use at such times when they
cannot be had otherwise; I come now to perform what I promised, and you
shall find me rather better than worse than my word.

That this may be done methodically, I shall divide my directions into
two grand sections, and each section into several chapters, and then
you shall see it look with such a countenance as this is.

pubmed.title: Digitalis.
pubmed.relevance_note: Reviews cardiac glycosides; notes historical use for dropsy and heart failure, not traditional wound or gynecological applications.

pubmed.title: Digitalis purpurea.
pubmed.relevance_note: Discusses toxicology and cardiac effects; lacks evidence supporting traditional uses for bloody flux, ulcers, or hair shedding.

pubmed.title: Clinical Use of Digitalis: A State of the Art Review.
pubmed.relevance_note: Focuses on modern cardiology; does not validate historical claims regarding inflammation, wounds, or reproductive health.

evidence.summary: Modern literature confirms potent cardiac glycosides but offers no evidence supporting traditional uses for women's health, bloody flux, ulcers, or hair loss. Historical applications likely relied on toxicity rather than therapeutic efficacy.

concordance.rationale: Digitalis purpurea is a potent cardiac glycoside with narrow therapeutic index; modern evidence flags severe toxicity (arrhythmias, death) and lacks support for wound healing or hair retention.
concordance.uncertainty: Low uncertainty regarding safety profile of Digitalis purpurea.
caveats: Historical uses likely involved different preparations or species.
Modern evidence focuses on cardiac toxicity.

issues: Unearned Grade D: The entry assigns a 'D' grade based on modern cardiac toxicity evidence for Digitalis purpurea. However, the historical claims (gonorrhea, wound healing) are not supported by EMA or clinical trials, yet the reasoning conflates modern safety profiles with historical efficacy without explicitly stating that the historical claims lack evidence. This creates an incoherence between the 'evidence' field (only 3 PubMed hits on toxicity) and the implied rejection of all historical uses.

Incomplete Resolution: The historical name 'Militaris' was selected as empty/ambiguous, but no alternative scientific name or specific reason for ambiguity beyond 'LLM proposal' is provided in the evidence, leaving the taxon unresolved.

Missing Evidence for Rejection: The grade 'D' (contradicts) implies a strong refutation of the entry's claims. While toxicity is real, the entry does not provide positive evidence *for* the historical uses to refute them, nor does it cite sources that specifically debunk the gonorrhea/wound healing claims in this context, relying solely on the existence of toxicity data which is insufficient to fully 'contradict' specific non-cardiac historical uses without further qualification.
